text.name: Article title
text.text:
Our first change
on the SP.

text.name: Description
text.text: How we traced a menu title from Roland's update files to the SP's screen, what we checked at each step, and how to repeat the offline checks.

text.name: Scope
text.text: The menu check after the candidate was installed.

text.name: Reconstruction label
text.text:
TITLE-ONLY RECONSTRUCTION
ILLUSTRATIVE TIMING / NO DEVICE CONNECTION

text.name: Replay status
text.text: Release the controls. This reconstructs the owner's reported observation.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We started with a question: how much of the SP could we change through its firmware? Roland's public updates gave us somewhere to look. Each archive contained two binaries, SP404MKII_APP0.bin and SP404MKII_APP1.bin. There was no source tree, SDK or board schematic alongside them.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Before touching the files, we kept the original archive, recorded its download URL and computed SHA-256 hashes for the archive and both binaries. A version label alone is not enough: two differently edited files can have the same name. We began with five releases and eventually compared eight, using version 5.52 as our working base.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: APP1 offered readable strings and recognizable ARM instructions. APP0 was much less transparent. Treating them as two parts to investigate, rather than assuming their filenames explained their jobs, kept the early guesses separate from what we actually knew.

text.name: File note 0
text.text: 2,359,296 bytes. Opaque body; role still under investigation.

text.name: File note 1
text.text: 2,652,672 bytes. Readable strings and ARM instructions.

text.name: Caption
text.text: Our preserved v5.52 inputs. Sizes identify the files; SHA-256 identifies their exact contents.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Obtain the official update from Roland and keep its archive unchanged. Extract a separate working copy; do not connect the SP for this reading exercise.

2. In the extracted folder, record each file's size and SHA-256. Compare with the v5.52 record below only if you have that exact release. A mismatch means stop and identify your input.

text.name: Command
text.text:
Get-Item .\SP404MKII_APP0.bin, .\SP404MKII_APP1.bin | Select-Object Name, Length
Get-FileHash .\SP404MKII_APP0.bin, .\SP404MKII_APP1.bin -Algorithm SHA256

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: You should have an untouched archive, two identified binaries and a small record of where they came from. The commands only read the files.

text.name: Heading
text.text: 2. Separate file bytes from runtime memory

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A binary is a long sequence of bytes. A running program needs those bytes in particular places. APP1's startup code described how to build that arrangement: copy some regions, decompress others and clear others to zero. This is called scatter loading.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We treated each startup region as a record: source in the file, destination in memory, length and operation. Copy preserves bytes; decompression expands a stored representation; zero-fill creates empty state that need not occupy space in the file. File offsets and runtime addresses therefore cannot be used interchangeably. We checked those regions before trusting references in IDA.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Our extractor initially assumed every firmware version had the same startup layout. The older releases proved otherwise. We corrected that assumption and a separate emulator stop-address mistake, then compared the extracted output with the original instructions. A tool failure had taught us to check the experiment as carefully as the firmware.

text.name: Motion status
text.text: The operations explain why a file offset is not a runtime address.

text.name: Caption
text.text: Copy, expansion and zero-fill do different jobs. The small letter sequences are illustrative, not bytes or addresses from the firmware.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Keep file offsets and runtime addresses in separate columns in your notes. Record how each region is produced before assigning it a purpose.

2. Use the timeline to compare the three operations. A region created by zero-fill has no block of stored bytes to search in the original file.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: Our runtime extraction was version-specific and checked against the original startup instructions. This diagram explains the result; it is not a loader or a complete recipe for rebuilding that memory map.

text.name: Heading
text.text: 3. Follow the title to its caller

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: With those regions in place, we used IDA and the ARM Hex-Rays decompiler to inspect the program. A decompiler translates machine instructions into C-like pseudocode. It makes relationships easier to follow, but it cannot give back the original names, comments or intent.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first full export produced pseudocode for 8,592 of 8,593 candidate functions. That was a useful map, with a known missing piece. Names such as sub_8013E8B0 were still address-based labels, and inferred types needed checking.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Readable text gave us an anchor. We found UTILITY MENU, followed its cross-reference into a function and inspected the call that consumed the title. The nearby SYSTEM label gave us a second clue that this was the Utility drawing route. We kept the decompiler's original address-based names in the excerpt so the source remains identifiable. One matching string alone would not have established that the visible menu used it.

text.name: Code
Code explanation
text.text: The title reference is passed to a drawing call. The familiar SYSTEM label below helps identify the menu.

text.name: Motion status
text.text: A reference connects the text to a consumer; execution tests check that route.

text.name: Caption
text.text: Actual IDA pseudocode, with omissions marked. The timeline follows the string reference, its drawing call and a nearby label that corroborates the menu's identity.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. In an already correctly mapped analysis database, open IDA's Strings view, select the menu title and inspect its cross-references. Open the referring function's pseudocode alongside its disassembly.

2. Check the argument carrying the title, then look for a second recognizable menu label in the same routine. If references land outside mapped regions, return to the mapping step instead of guessing.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: Our anchor was aUtilityMenu in the title-drawing call, with SYSTEM nearby. The excerpt below can be inspected without IDA; it does not reconstruct the whole database.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The initial ambition was much bigger than a menu label. We built an original diagnostic program and investigated how a replacement application might start. The monitor passed instruction-level tests, but it had not run on the SP. The resident loader's full contract was still unknown.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: That was a real obstacle to a complete replacement. It did not mean every smaller experiment had to wait. On September 22, the direction became explicit: start with a visible proof of concept.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The stock system already knew how to start the instrument and draw its menus. Could we leave that machinery alone and change one piece of text?

text.name: Caption
text.text: A small experiment needs an explicit boundary and an observable result.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Write down the one observation that would count as success: the Utility menu displays CUSTOM MENU!.

2. List what must remain unchanged: APP0, APP1 length, the title's terminator, surrounding bytes and the other menu-drawing behavior.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: A changed title would answer whether this candidate reached the visible menu. It would not demonstrate a replacement OS or a recovery method.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: UTILITY MENU and CUSTOM MENU! both contain twelve printable characters. That let the experiment keep the terminating zero, image size and surrounding layout intact. APP0 stayed byte-for-byte unchanged; the only changed APP1 positions were the twelve title bytes.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: It was a small result by design. A recognizable title would tell us whether this specific modified image had reached a visible part of the interface. It would not prove that a replacement operating system, audio engine or recovery path worked.

text.name: Characters 0
text.text: U  T  I  L  I  T  Y  ·  M  E  N  U  NUL

text.name: Characters 1
text.text: C  U  S  T  O  M  ·  M  E  N  U  !  NUL

text.name: Motion status
text.text: 12 changed bytes. The zero terminator and total length are unchanged.

text.name: Caption
text.text: A comparison of the two title records, including the unchanged zero terminator. Scrubbing reveals the comparison; it does not edit or install firmware.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Count bytes, not just visible characters. These titles use ASCII: twelve printable bytes followed by a zero terminator. The space is a byte too.

2. Run the downloadable offline example with Python 3. It constructs two tiny records in memory, checks their lengths and terminators, and confirms that reversing the replacement restores the original record.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: Expected output: 12 changed bytes; terminator unchanged; size unchanged; reverse comparison passed. This synthetic example accepts no input files and is not an SP firmware patcher.

text.name: Heading
text.text: 6. Test the consumer, not just the string

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Finding the new words in the output file was only the first check. We ran the stock memory-copy instructions and Utility drawing routine in an instruction-level emulator, once for each of six selections in both the original and modified images.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The test compared the drawing calls produced by each run: expected title, other labels, icon states and selected item. All twelve cases reached the expected title-drawing call, with the other observations consistent. A fresh rebuild produced identical bytes; reversing the title change restored the original APP1 hash. These checked different failure modes: reproducibility, scope of change and the route actually consuming the text.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Those checks supported the experiment without pretending to be a device test. The package still carried UNVERIFIED in its name when it left the PC. Acceptance by the updater and the actual display result were still unanswered.

text.name: Motion status
text.text: 12 of 12 recorded CPU cases passed. Hardware was a separate check.

text.name: Caption
text.text: Replay of the preserved CPU-test report: six selections for each image. This animation is not running an emulator or testing connected hardware.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Separate file checks from execution checks. A text search can confirm that a title exists; it cannot confirm which code path displays it.

2. In the offline example, inspect the six-selection by two-title test matrix. It demonstrates the comparison structure with an original Python model, not the SP's machine instructions.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: The example should report 12 synthetic cases passed. Our historical report contains 12 instruction-level menu cases. Those are different tests; neither is a physical-device result.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We did not yet have a verified USB flashing path. The owner installed the candidate through the SD update workflow, then checked the Utility menu using SHIFT and pad 13. The expected title was CUSTOM MENU!.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The reply was short: “it wokred”. On September 22, we recorded the first owner-reported visible success. The supplied stock-based modification had made it to the instrument and produced the expected result.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: There was no independent screen capture or installed-image readback, so the record stays precise about its evidence. This was a reported success for one particular title change. The larger questions remained, but the next experiment could start from something that had worked on the SP.

text.name: Evidence scope
text.text: Reported visible success. No independent screen capture or installed-image readback.

text.name: Caption
text.text: The observation expected after the candidate was installed. SHIFT and pad 13 open the menu; pressing them does not perform the title modification.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Keep the supplied candidate's identity separate from a device readback. We preserved the candidate hash, but did not independently capture the installed bytes.

2. Record what the owner actually observed and what remains untested. Preserve the exact reply and do not relabel the earlier CPU checks as hardware tests.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: The offline reproduction ends here. The historical owner report supports this one visible result; this page does not provide an installation package or establish recovery after a failed update.

text.name: Evidence text
text.text: The preserved download manifest, IDA export summary, menu-test report and September 22 hardware note underpin this account. Read the curated evidence record.

text.name: References
text.text: References: Roland’s official update index · Project source ledger

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. In an already correctly mapped analysis database, open IDA's Strings view, select the menu title and inspect its cross-references. Open the referring function's pseudocode alongside its disassembly.

2. Check the argument carrying the title, then look for a second recognizable menu label in the same routine. If references land outside mapped regions, return to the mapping step instead of guessing.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: Our anchor was aUtilityMenu in the title-drawing call, with SYSTEM nearby. The excerpt below can be inspected without IDA; it does not reconstruct the whole database.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The initial ambition was much bigger than a menu label. We built an original diagnostic program and investigated how a replacement application might start. The monitor passed instruction-level tests, but it had not run on the SP. The resident loader's full contract was still unknown.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: That was a real obstacle to a complete replacement. It did not mean every smaller experiment had to wait. On September 22, the direction became explicit: start with a visible proof of concept.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The stock system already knew how to start the instrument and draw its menus. Could we leave that machinery alone and change one piece of text?

text.name: Caption
text.text: A small experiment needs an explicit boundary and an observable result.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Write down the one observation that would count as success: the Utility menu displays CUSTOM MENU!.

2. List what must remain unchanged: APP0, APP1 length, the title's terminator, surrounding bytes and the other menu-drawing behavior.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: A changed title would answer whether this candidate reached the visible menu. It would not demonstrate a replacement OS or a recovery method.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: UTILITY MENU and CUSTOM MENU! both contain twelve printable characters. That let the experiment keep the terminating zero, image size and surrounding layout intact. APP0 stayed byte-for-byte unchanged; the only changed APP1 positions were the twelve title bytes.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: It was a small result by design. A recognizable title would tell us whether this specific modified image had reached a visible part of the interface. It would not prove that a replacement operating system, audio engine or recovery path worked.

text.text: A comparison of the two title records, including the unchanged zero terminator. Scrubbing reveals the comparison; it does not edit or install firmware.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Count bytes, not just visible characters. These titles use ASCII: twelve printable bytes followed by a zero terminator. The space is a byte too.

2. Run the downloadable offline example with Python 3. It constructs two tiny records in memory, checks their lengths and terminators, and confirms that reversing the replacement restores the original record.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: Expected output: 12 changed bytes; terminator unchanged; size unchanged; reverse comparison passed. This synthetic example accepts no input files and is not an SP firmware patcher.

text.name: Heading
text.text: 6. Test the consumer, not just the string

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Finding the new words in the output file was only the first check. We ran the stock memory-copy instructions and Utility drawing routine in an instruction-level emulator, once for each of six selections in both the original and modified images.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The test compared the drawing calls produced by each run: expected title, other labels, icon states and selected item. All twelve cases reached the expected title-drawing call, with the other observations consistent. A fresh rebuild produced identical bytes; reversing the title change restored the original APP1 hash. These checked different failure modes: reproducibility, scope of change and the route actually consuming the text.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Those checks supported the experiment without pretending to be a device test. The package still carried UNVERIFIED in its name when it left the PC. Acceptance by the updater and the actual display result were still unanswered.

text.text: We did not yet have a verified USB flashing path. The owner installed the candidate through the SD update workflow, then checked the Utility menu using SHIFT and pad 13. The expected title was CUSTOM MENU!.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The reply was short: “it wokred”. On September 22, we recorded the first owner-reported visible success. The supplied stock-based modification had made it to the instrument and produced the expected result.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: There was no independent screen capture or installed-image readback, so the record stays precise about its evidence. This was a reported success for one particular title change. The larger questions remained, but the next experiment could start from something that had worked on the SP.

text.name: Article title
text.text:
Our first change
on the SP.

text.name: Description
text.text: How we traced a menu title from Roland's update files to the SP's screen, what we checked at each step, and how to repeat the offline checks.

text.name: Scope
text.text: The menu check after the candidate was installed.

text.name: Reconstruction label
text.text:
TITLE-ONLY RECONSTRUCTION
ILLUSTRATIVE TIMING / NO DEVICE CONNECTION

text.name: Replay status
text.text: Release the controls. This reconstructs the owner's reported observation.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We started with a question: how much of the SP could we change through its firmware? Roland's public updates gave us somewhere to look. Each archive contained two binaries, SP404MKII_APP0.bin and SP404MKII_APP1.bin. There was no source tree, SDK or board schematic alongside them.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Before touching the files, we kept the original archive, recorded its download URL and computed SHA-256 hashes for the archive and both binaries. A version label alone is not enough: two differently edited files can have the same name. We began with five releases and eventually compared eight, using version 5.52 as our working base.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: APP1 offered readable strings and recognizable ARM instructions. APP0 was much less transparent. Treating them as two parts to investigate, rather than assuming their filenames explained their jobs, kept the early guesses separate from what we actually knew.

text.name: File note 0
text.text: 2,359,296 bytes. Opaque body; role still under investigation.

text.name: File note 1
text.text: 2,652,672 bytes. Readable strings and ARM instructions.

text.name: Caption
text.text: Our preserved v5.52 inputs. Sizes identify the files; SHA-256 identifies their exact contents.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Obtain the official update from Roland and keep its archive unchanged. Extract a separate working copy; do not connect the SP for this reading exercise.

2. In the extracted folder, record each file's size and SHA-256. Compare with the v5.52 record below only if you have that exact release. A mismatch means stop and identify your input.

text.name: Command
text.text:
Get-Item .\SP404MKII_APP0.bin, .\SP404MKII_APP1.bin | Select-Object Name, Length
Get-FileHash .\SP404MKII_APP0.bin, .\SP404MKII_APP1.bin -Algorithm SHA256

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: You should have an untouched archive, two identified binaries and a small record of where they came from. The commands only read the files.

text.name: Heading
text.text: 2. Separate file bytes from runtime memory

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: A binary is a long sequence of bytes. A running program needs those bytes in particular places. APP1's startup code described how to build that arrangement: copy some regions, decompress others and clear others to zero. This is called scatter loading.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: We treated each startup region as a record: source in the file, destination in memory, length and operation. Copy preserves bytes; decompression expands a stored representation; zero-fill creates empty state that need not occupy space in the file. File offsets and runtime addresses therefore cannot be used interchangeably. We checked those regions before trusting references in IDA.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Our extractor initially assumed every firmware version had the same startup layout. The older releases proved otherwise. We corrected that assumption and a separate emulator stop-address mistake, then compared the extracted output with the original instructions. A tool failure had taught us to check the experiment as carefully as the firmware.

text.name: Motion status
text.text: The operations explain why a file offset is not a runtime address.

text.name: Caption
text.text: Copy, expansion and zero-fill do different jobs. The small letter sequences are illustrative, not bytes or addresses from the firmware.

text.name: Steps
text.text:
1. Keep file offsets and runtime addresses in separate columns in your notes. Record how each region is produced before assigning it a purpose.

2. Use the timeline to compare the three operations. A region created by zero-fill has no block of stored bytes to search in the original file.

text.name: Checkpoint note
text.text: Our runtime extraction was version-specific and checked against the original startup instructions. This diagram explains the result; it is not a loader or a complete recipe for rebuilding that memory map.

text.name: Heading
text.text: 3. Follow the title to its caller

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: With those regions in place, we used IDA and the ARM Hex-Rays decompiler to inspect the program. A decompiler translates machine instructions into C-like pseudocode. It makes relationships easier to follow, but it cannot give back the original names, comments or intent.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: The first full export produced pseudocode for 8,592 of 8,593 candidate functions. That was a useful map, with a known missing piece. Names such as sub_8013E8B0 were still address-based labels, and inferred types needed checking.

text.name: Paragraph
text.text: Readable text gave us an anchor. We found UTILITY MENU, followed its cross-reference into a function and inspected the call that consumed the title. The nearby SYSTEM label gave us a second clue that this was the Utility drawing route. We kept the decompiler's original address-based names in the excerpt so the source remains identifiable. One matching string alone would not have established that the visible menu used it.

Code explanation
